data.title: Dynagas LNG Partners LP Reports Results for the Three and Nine Months Ended September 30, 2026
data.description:
ATHENS, Greece, Nov. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Dynagas LNG Partners LP (NYSE: DLNG) (the “Partnership”), an owner of liquefied natural gas (“LNG”) carriers, today announced its results for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026.

Nine Months Highlights:

  • Net Income and Earnings per common unit (basic and diluted) of $51.9 million and $1.29, respectively;
  • Adjusted Net Income(1) of $46.6 million and Adjusted Earnings per common unit(1) (basic and diluted) of $1.14;
  • Adjusted EBITDA(1) of $82.0 million; and
  • 97.1% fleet utilization(2).

Quarter Highlights:

  • Net Income and Earnings per common unit (basic and diluted) of $18.6 million and $0.46, respectively;
  • Adjusted Net Income(1) of $18.4 million and Adjusted Earnings per common unit(1) (basic and diluted) of $0.46;
  • Adjusted EBITDA(1) of $30.1 million;
  • 100% fleet utilization(2);
  • The Arctic Aurora was delivered under its new time charter party agreement with Rio Grande LNG, LLC (“Rio Grande”) on September 15, 2026;
  • Declared and paid a cash distribution of $0.5625 per unit on the Partnership’s Series A Preferred Units (NYSE: DLNG PR A) for the period from May 12, 2026 to August 11, 2026; and
  • Declared a quarterly cash distribution of $0.050 per common unit for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, which was paid on August 28, 2026, to all common unitholders of record as of August 24, 2026.

(1) Adjusted Net Income, Adjusted Earnings per common unit and Adjusted EBITDA are not recognized measures under U.S. GAAP. Please refer to Appendix B of this press release for the definitions and reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable financial measures calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP and other related information.
(2) Please refer to Appendix B for additional information on how the Partnership calculates fleet utilization.

Recent Events: 

  • On November 12, 2026, the Partnership completed the partial redemption of its Series A Preferred Units, redeeming 2,000,000 of its 3,000,000 outstanding Series A Preferred Units, which was announced on October 9, 2026, at a redemption price of $25.00 per unit, or $50.0 million in aggregate. Following the partial redemption, 1,000,000 Series A Preferred Units remain outstanding;
  • Declared a quarterly cash distribution of $0.5625 per unit on the Partnership’s Series A Preferred Units for the period from August 12, 2026 to November 11, 2026, which was paid on November 12, 2026 to all Series A Preferred unitholders of record as of November 4, 2026; and
  • Declared a quarterly cash distribution of $0.050 per common unit for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, which is payable on November 20, 2026 to all common unitholders of record as of November 13, 2026.
  • For an update on the current status and potential impact on us of applicable sanctions, please see “Russian Sanctions Developments” below.

CEO Commentary:

We are pleased to report a strong third quarter. Adjusted EBITDA rose 9.2% year on year to $30.1 million and Adjusted Net Income increased 29.3% to $18.4 million, as the fleet operated at 100% utilization and our fleet-wide Time Charter Equivalent (TCE) rate reached $75,027 per day, up 11.8% on the third quarter of 2025 and 7.0% on the previous quarter. This TCE comfortably exceeded our cash breakeven for the quarter of approximately $47,100 per day. The quarter benefited from the first full three months of the Clean Energy’s charter with Rio Grande and from a further 30.8% year-on-year reduction in net interest and finance costs.

Commercially, the Arctic Aurora commenced its new time charter with Rio Grande on September 15, 2026, securing its employment until at least August 2033. With two of our six vessels now chartered to Rio Grande, alongside our long-standing charters with SEFE and Yamal Trade, our fleet is fully contracted for the remainder of 2026 and for 2027, and 65% contracted for 2028. As of the date of this release, our estimated contracted revenue backlog stands at $700 million, with an average remaining contract term of 4.2 years.

Our balance sheet continued to strengthen. During the first nine months of 2026 we repaid $33.1 million of debt, reducing our outstanding financial liabilities to $245.6 million, while our cash increased to $79.9 million at September 30, 2026 from $41.0 million at the end of 2025. At the same time, we continued to return capital to our unitholders, maintaining our quarterly distribution of $0.050 per common unit and paying the full distributions on our Series A Preferred Units. After the quarter end, on November 12, 2026, we redeemed 2,000,000 of our Series A Preferred Units, two-thirds of the class, for $50.0 million, which reduces our annual preferred distributions by $4.5 million.

Three Months Ended September 30, 2026 and 2025 Financial Results

Net Income for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was $18.6 million as compared to $18.7 million for the corresponding period in 2025, which represents a decrease of $0.1 million, or 0.6%. The decrease in Net Income was mainly attributable to the Other income which was recognized in the third quarter of 2025, and the increase in Voyage expenses and Vessel operating expenses. The above decrease was substantially offset by (a) the increase in Voyage revenues and (b) the decrease in Net interest and finance costs as explained below.

Adjusted Net Income (a non-GAAP financial measure) for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was $18.4 million, compared to $14.2 million for the corresponding period in 2025, which represents a net increase of $4.2 million, or 29.3%. This increase was mainly attributable to (a) the increase in cash Voyage revenues as explained below, and (b) the decrease in Net interest and finance costs which was partially offset by the increase in Vessel operating expenses.

Voyage revenues for the three months ended September 30, 2026 were $44.0 million, compared to $38.9 million for the corresponding period in 2025, which represents a net increase of $5.1 million, or 13.1%. This increase was mainly attributable to: (a) the higher time charter rate earned by the Clean Energy under its time charter with Rio Grande, which commenced on April 30, 2026, (b) the increase in variable hire revenues earned under the OPEX pass-through time charters of the Yenisei River and the Lena River, (c) the increase in Revenue earning days, as the fleet operated at full utilization during the quarter compared to the corresponding period of 2025, (d) the non-cash effect of the amortization of deferred revenue, (e) a ballast bonus of $0.9 million due to the Partnership upon the redelivery of the Arctic Aurora by Equinor and (f) the increase of the value of the EU ETS emissions allowances (“EUAs”) due to the Partnership by the charterers of its vessels (the corresponding value of the EUAs, which the Partnership is obliged to surrender to the EU authorities, is included within Voyage expenses, therefore the net effect of the EUAs to the Operating Income and Net income is zero). The above increase was partially offset by the lower time charter rates earned by the Arctic Aurora under its charter with Equinor until September 15, 2026 and under its new time charter thereafter, compared to the corresponding period in 2025.

The Partnership reported average daily hire gross of commissions(3) of approximately $74,820 per day per vessel for the three-month period ended September 30, 2026, compared to approximately $69,960 per day per vessel for the corresponding period in 2025. The Partnership’s vessels operated at 100% and 99.1% fleet utilization during the three-month periods ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively.

Vessel operating expenses were $8.9 million, which corresponds to a daily rate per vessel of $16,121 for the three-month period ended September 30, 2026, compared to $8.1 million, or a daily rate per vessel of $14,594 in the corresponding period in 2025. This increase was mainly attributable to increased crew costs and higher repairs and maintenance costs. As mentioned above, a substantial part of the increase in Vessel operating expenses is counter-balanced by the corresponding increase in variable hire revenues earned on the Partnership’s vessels operating under OPEX pass-through time charters.

Adjusted EBITDA (a non-GAAP financial measure) for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was $30.1 million, compared to $27.6 million for the corresponding period in 2025. The increase of $2.5 million, or 9.2%, was mainly attributable to the above-mentioned increase in cash Voyage revenues, which was partially offset by the increase in Vessel operating expenses.

Net interest and finance costs were $3.7 million in the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared to $5.3 million in the corresponding period in 2025, which represents a decrease of $1.6 million, or 30.8%, mainly due to (i) the decrease in the interest on our Sale and Leaseback Agreements, as a result of the reduction in interest-bearing debt and the decrease in the weighted average interest rate from 6.50% in the three months ended September 30, 2025 to 5.94% in the three months ended September 30, 2026, (ii) the interest expense of $0.4 million on the Series B Preferred Units for the period from July 1, 2025 to their redemption date on July 25, 2025, which was included in the corresponding period of 2025, and (iii) the increase in interest income.

For the three months ended September 30, 2026, the Partnership reported both basic and diluted Earnings per common unit and Adjusted Earnings per common unit (a non-GAAP financial measure), of $0.46, after taking into account the distributions relating to the Series A Preferred Units on the Partnership’s Net Income/Adjusted Net Income. Earnings per common unit and Adjusted Earnings per common unit, basic and diluted, were calculated on the basis of a weighted average number of 36,382,011 common units outstanding during the period and in the case of Adjusted Earnings per common unit, after reflecting the impact of certain adjustments presented in Appendix B of this press release.

Adjusted Net Income, Adjusted EBITDA, and Adjusted Earnings per common unit are not recognized measures under U.S. GAAP. Please refer to Appendix B of this press release for the definitions and reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable financial measures calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP.

Liquidity/ Financing/ Cash Flow Coverage

During the three months ended September 30, 2026, the Partnership generated net cash from operating activities of $35.0 million, compared to $26.5 million in the corresponding period in 2025, which represents an increase of $8.5 million, or 32.0%, mainly as a result of working capital changes.

As of September 30, 2026, the Partnership reported total cash of $79.9 million. The Partnership’s outstanding financial liabilities as of September 30, 2026, under the Sale and Leaseback Agreements between the vessel owning companies of the Clean Energy, the OB River, the Amur River and the Arctic Aurora and China Development Bank Financial Leasing Co. Ltd. amounted to $34.3 million, $45.6 million, $46.8 million and $118.9 million, respectively, gross of unamortized deferred loan fees. The financial liabilities under the Sale and Leaseback Agreements are repayable in quarterly installments, with the final installments, including purchase obligation prices of $10.7 million, $14.2 million, $14.6 million and $22.1 million, respectively, due in June 2029 for the Clean Energy, the OB River and the Amur River and in June 2034 for the Arctic Aurora. During the three months ended September 30, 2026, the Partnership repaid $11.0 million of its financial liabilities and paid distributions of $3.5 million to its preferred and common unitholders. Scheduled principal repayments for the twelve months ending September 30, 2027 amount to $44.2 million.

On November 12, 2026, the Partnership paid $50.0 million for the partial redemption of its Series A Preferred Units described under “Recent Events” above.

Vessel Employment

As of November 20, 2026, the Partnership had estimated contracted time charter coverage(4) for 100%, 100% and 65% of its fleet estimated Available Days (as defined in Appendix B) for each of 2026, 2027 and 2028, respectively.

As of the same date, the Partnership’s estimated contracted revenue backlog (5) (6) was $700 million, with an average remaining contract term of 4.2 years.

(4) Time charter coverage for the Partnership’s fleet is calculated by dividing the fleet contracted days on the basis of the earliest estimated delivery and redelivery dates prescribed in the Partnership’s current time charter contracts, net of scheduled class survey repairs, by the number of expected Available Days during that period.

(5) The Partnership calculates its estimated contracted revenue backlog by multiplying the contractual daily hire rate by the expected number of days committed under the contracts (assuming earliest delivery and redelivery and excluding options to extend), assuming full utilization. The actual amount of revenues earned and the actual periods during which revenues are earned may differ from the amounts and periods disclosed due to, for example, the early termination or temporary suspension of charters, dry-docking and/or special survey downtime, maintenance projects, off-hire downtime and other factors that result in lower revenues than the Partnership’s estimated contracted revenue backlog.

(6) $87 million of the estimated contracted revenue backlog relates to the estimated portion of the hire contained in certain time charter contracts with Yamal Trade Pte. Ltd., which represents the operating expenses of the respective vessels and is subject to yearly adjustments on the basis of the actual operating costs incurred within each year. The actual amount of revenues earned in respect of such variable hire rate may therefore differ from the amounts included in the estimated contracted revenue backlog due to the yearly variations in the respective vessel’s operating costs.

Russian Sanctions Developments

Due to the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine, the United Kingdom (the “U.K.”), the European Union (“E.U.”), the United States (“U.S.”) and other countries and organizations have publicly announced and enacted extensive sanctions against Russia to impose severe economic pressure on the Russian economy and government.

Two of our vessels, the Yenisei River and Lena River (the “Vessels”), are employed by Yamal Trade Pte. Ltd. (the “Charterer”) under long-term time charters that extend to 2033 and 2034, respectively (the “Yamal Charters”). Since the commencement of the Yamal Charters, the Vessels have been engaged in the transportation of LNG produced in Russia for discharge at destinations worldwide (the “Yamal LNG Transportation”) in compliance with applicable sanctions regulations.

U.K. Sanctions

On May 20, 2026, the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/543) came into force in the U.K., amending the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. The amendments introduced new Regulations 46Z29B to 46Z29D, which prohibit U.K. persons from directly or indirectly supplying or delivering Russian-origin LNG by ship, and from providing or facilitating related services. The ban covers shipments from Russia to third countries as well as between third countries and is subject to limited exceptions and licensing arrangements. For supply contracts with a duration exceeding one year that were executed before June 17, 2025 and have not since been amended, other than by amendments falling within specified categories, there is a transitional exception that covers relevant activities carried out before January 1, 2027.

As a result, following expiry of the applicable transitional exception, U.K.-based providers of financial services, including the insurers that currently provide protection and indemnity (“P&I”) and hull and machinery (“H&M”) insurance for the Vessels, will be prohibited from providing cover for voyages carrying Russian-origin LNG, unless an applicable exception or licence permits such cover. The U.K. prohibition does not extend to technical services, including classification.

As of the date of this press release, discussions with alternative insurance providers are ongoing; however, we have not secured replacement P&I or H&M insurance for the Vessels and there can be no assurance that such insurance will be in place by January 1, 2027, or that it will be available on comparable terms, or at all. If such insurance is not in place, this could give rise to disputes under the Yamal Charters, including disputes concerning the respective rights and obligations of the Charterer and us under the Yamal Charters. Any such dispute could result in claims that the Vessels are off-hire, additional costs, loss of revenue, litigation or early termination of the Yamal Charters, among other things. Any of these developments could adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows and our ability to make distributions to our unitholders and could result in an event of default under our debt agreements, among other things.

E.U. Sanctions

On October 23, 2025, the E.U. adopted the 19th package of sanctions (the “19th Package”), which prohibits the purchase, import or transfer, directly or indirectly, by E.U. persons and non-E.U. persons with an E.U.-nexus, of LNG that originates in Russia or is exported from Russia (the “LNG Prohibition”). The LNG Prohibition applies from January 1, 2027 with respect to supply contracts with a duration exceeding one year (“Long Term Contracts”) that were executed before June 17, 2025 and that have not since been amended, other than by amendments falling within specified categories.

On July 23, 2026, the E.U. amended the 19th Package with the adoption of the 21st package of sanctions (the “21st Package”). The 21st Package introduced an exemption to the LNG Prohibition, initially until July 25, 2027, and thereafter for successive periods of one year, unless the Council of the E.U. (the “E.U. Council”), following an annual review, decides otherwise. The exemption applies to transfers of LNG destined for third countries and, where relevant, purchases associated with those transfers, pursuant to Long Term Contracts that were executed before February 24, 2022 and that have not since been amended, other than by amendments falling within specified categories, provided that the volume of LNG transferred each year under the exemption does not exceed the volume of LNG transferred in 2025 under its qualifying existing Long Term Contract, irrespective of destination (the “Legacy Contract Derogation”).

We, and our sanctions counsel, believe that the transportation of LNG under the Yamal Charters to destinations outside the E.U. currently falls within the Legacy Contract Derogation and, accordingly, is outside the scope of the LNG Prohibition. However, there can be no absolute guaranteed assurance that our interpretation of the Legacy Contract Derogation is correct, or that regulatory authorities or our counterparties will agree with our interpretation. Furthermore, there can be no absolute guaranteed assurance that the transportation of LNG under the Yamal Charters will continue to meet the requirements of the Legacy Contract Derogation, including with respect to the yearly volume limitation, or that the E.U. Council will not decide, following an annual review, to shorten or terminate the Legacy Contract Derogation, or that sanctions regulations will not be further implemented, amended, or expanded to restrict the transportation of Russian-origin LNG.

These risks are outside of our control, and if one or more of these events were to occur, the Vessels would be restricted from transporting LNG originating in or exported from Russia, which would affect the Charterer’s ability to continue employing the Vessels in the Yamal LNG Transportation. Notwithstanding the foregoing, we believe the Yamal Charters would remain enforceable, although their sanctions-specific provisions may suspend performance and, at a later stage, payment of charter hire. The Charterer may not agree with our interpretation, which could result in disputes, Charterer non-performance, litigation or early termination of the Yamal Charters, among other things. Any of these developments would have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, financial condition, cash flows and our ability to make distributions to our unitholders and could result in an event of default under our debt agreements, among other things.

U.S. Sanctions

On September 18, 2026, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (the “Graham Act”) was enacted in the U.S. Among other things, the Graham Act authorizes the President to impose sanctions on foreign vessels that the President determines knowingly transport LNG or certain other energy products originating in Russia, and on persons that provide services to such vessels. On October 16, 2026, the President issued Executive Order 14436, which waived the application of the sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for in the Graham Act. The waiver has no fixed expiration date, and it may be revoked or modified at any time. No sanctions have been imposed on us or the Vessels under the Graham Act. However, there can be no assurance that the waiver will remain in effect, or that sanctions will not be imposed under the Graham Act on us, the Vessels, the Charterer or our service providers, which could restrict or prevent the employment of the Vessels under the Yamal Charters and affect our access to insurance, financing and other services.

General

Our fleet consists of only six LNG carriers and we derive all our revenues from a limited number of charterers. For the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026, the Charterer accounted for approximately 34% of our total revenues, and the charter revenue expected to be generated by the Yamal Charters constituted approximately 56% of our estimated contract backlog. The loss of revenue under either or both of the Yamal Charters would have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, financial condition, cash flows and our ability to make distributions to our unitholders, and could result in an event of default under our debt agreements.

Other than as described above in relation to the U.K. regulations, applicable U.S., U.K. and E.U. sanctions regimes that are in effect as of the date of this press release do not materially affect our business, operations or financial condition and, to our knowledge, our counterparties are currently performing their obligations under their respective time charters. We closely monitor the applicability of sanctions regulations on us and our counterparties, and the potential impact of economic sanctions on our existing commercial arrangements, including the Yamal Charters. The full impact of the commercial and economic consequences of the Russian war with Ukraine is uncertain at this time. The U.K., E.U. and U.S. measures described above or any further development in sanctions, or escalation of the Ukraine war and other geopolitical events and conflicts more generally may have a material adverse impact on our business, results of operations, financial condition, cash flows, our ability to make distributions to unitholders or our ability to comply with the covenants in our debt agreements. Sanctions have been expanded over time and may continue to evolve and could ultimately restrict or prevent the performance of certain contractual obligations under our charters.

Please see the risk factors we describe in our Annual Report on Form 20-F for the year ended December 31, 2025, including without limitation, the risk factors entitled “We currently derive all our revenue and cash flow from a limited number of charterers and the loss of any of these charterers could cause us to suffer losses or otherwise adversely affect our business,” “Any charter termination would likely have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows,” “If our vessels call on ports located in countries or territories that are the subject of sanctions or embargoes imposed by the United States government or other governmental authorities, it could result in the imposition of monetary fines or penalties and adversely affect our reputation and the market for our securities” and “We may be subject to litigation that could have an adverse effect on us.”

About Dynagas LNG Partners LP

data.title: Grain Futures Finish Mixed to End Shaky Week for Commodities — Daily Grain Highlights
data.description:
By Anthony Harrup

--Corn for March delivery fell 0.8% Friday on the Chicago Board of Trade to $4.48 3/4 a bushel, closing out a negative week for commodities with losses.

--Wheat for March delivery declined 0.5% to $5.92 a bushel.

--Soybeans for January delivery rose 1.1% to $12.20 3/4 a bushel.

HIGHLIGHTS

No Risk Premium: Grains trading is likely to remain choppy in the short term as markets tussle with currency issues, South American weather and changes in global trade flows with no Russia-Ukraine peace deal likely, AgResource said in a note. "ARC maintains there's little to no risk premium in grains markets currently, and the assumption is that geopolitics and South American weather progress smoothly through the balance of 2026," the firm said. They also added that it won't take much in the way of shifting grain flows or weather scares in South America to give prices a boost.

Forecast Tweak: The International Grains Council raised its 2026/27 global production estimate for wheat and coarse grains by 1 million metric tons to 2.428 billion tons, with higher wheat and barley numbers offsetting lower corn. The biggest changes were increases for Turkey, Australia and Argentina, and a reduction for the U.S., the IGC says. Ending grain stocks are raised by 7 million tons to 626 million tons, "inflated by unusually heavy inventories in Russia and Ukraine." Soybean production is seen at 439 million tons, unchanged from the October forecast.

Flash Sale: The USDA reported sales of 100,000 metric tons of soybean cake and meal for delivery to Spain during the 2026/2027 marketing year.

INSIGHT

Bears vs. Bulls: Corn futures typically rise between Thanksgiving and year-end, with the March contract making an average gain of 32 cents a bushel between Nov. 20 and Dec. 31 in the past 12 years, Naomi Blohm of Total Farm Marketing said in a note.

"The old expression for grains: 'the bears get Thanksgiving, but the bulls get Christmas' may have rung true with the lower price action this November," she said. While each year has its own fundamental supply and demand perspectives, the March contract has had some sort of rally during the period since 2014. Some lasted only days, but others stretched to weeks.

Looking Up: Citi Research maintains a positive view on a number of agricultural commodities including corn and soybeans, and sees the recent drawdown as a buying opportunity. "We still expect El Niño to have larger impact on yields in the next 3-6 months," global head of commodities research Max Layton said in a note. Markets will also start taking notice of the Black Sea closure as Ukraine typically ramps up exports during this time of year. "Exports of both corn and soy have been relatively strong and we expect China delivering on their commitments on buying U.S. soy and potentially corn," Layton added.

data.title: SEC Proposes to Bring Securities Reporting Platform Under Direct Supervision
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

The Securities and Exchange Commission is proposing to restructure the system where securities exchanges report trading data.

The proposal aims to change the Consolidated Audit Trail, which is a centralized database that tracks trading activity across securities exchanges.

The SEC has proposed to rescind Rule 613, which requires securities exchanges to report their trading activity to the CAT. In its place, the SEC proposes to require exchanges to report the same information directly to the SEC or its designee.

The move would bring the CAT under the SEC's direct control.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins has been reviewing the CAT and approving amendments that have reduced its annual operating costs by more than $100 million. Atkins has also permanently eliminated the reporting of personally identifiable information to the CAT.

The proposal addresses concerns about the CAT's funding and would put the database on sustainable footing, Atkins said.

data.title: My husband spent $80,000 on a boat, yet says my plans for a $100,000 pottery studio are irresponsible. Who's right?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'We have $2.9 million in retirement accounts. That includes some money that we inherited about 10 years ago.'

"My husband, however, is skeptical. He says that's a lot of money to spend on something that I'm trying to profit from." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My husband and I have been married for 31 years. He's 65 and I'm 62. I work part-time in a dental office and we have a house that's fully paid off. It's worth about $900,000. Best of all, we have $2.9 million in retirement accounts. That includes some money that we inherited about 10 years ago.

For the last 15 years, I have dreamed of opening my own pottery studio. I've taken lessons at our Saturday market for several years, and I find it extremely meditative and also a wonderful pastime. There's a space near an old rail depot, about 900 square feet, which would be perfect for a pottery studio, where I could teach others. By my estimations, insurance, equipment and rent would require about $100,000.

My husband, however, is skeptical. He says that's a lot of money to spend on something that I'm trying to profit from. My sister says it's bad timing given that we're both heading into retirement. Three years ago, he purchased a boat for $80,000 and spent $12,000 on a new motor and fishfinder. He barely used it, and finally sold it at a loss.

I'm not claiming my pottery studio will make us rich, but I'm perfectly willing to come up with a business plan and set a budget, with a red line on the amount of money I would be prepared to lose. I'd actually also start a lot smaller and build up if the price is right. We could have 30 years ahead of us in retirement, and I want to spend it doing something that brings me a lot of joy.

Am I being unrealistic?

A 62-Year-Old Wife

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I like the idea of a big return': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?

Tell your husband that you're not giving up before you've even started.

Dear Wife,

From your letter, it doesn't sound like pottery is just a business for you.

For you, pottery is a passion, and it's important to have something you like doing in retirement. If you are going to choose to open a business, it should be something you will love because it won't always be easy, and you may need to rely on that bedrock of belief when the going gets tough. That's in addition to financial projections, advice from an accountant, knowing where you draw a hard line on the budget if sales dry up, and even a Plan B for the space.

I'm not going to tell you to open a business and spend $100,000, which could be a little on the high side, although you will know more when you compare this plan to similar-sized businesses and complete your due diligence. More important, I'm not going to tell you not to do it, and I don't think anyone else should, either, at least not without hearing you out, visiting the proposed site and, crucially, seeing your business plan. What stands out from your letter is your husband's immediate, possibly knee-jerk, opposition.

However, pointing out that he bought an $80,000 motorboat and ended up throwing good money after bad and selling it at a loss may be fair, but it doesn't help your cause. Yes, he decided to pursue something that he eventually tired of or decided wasn't worth all the hassle and expense. He's the one who apparently lost interest in a project after spending nearly six figures, not you. But it won't help to trade successes and failures in a tit-for-tat argument.

If a pottery studio is a vocation, you have earned the right to at least look into it.

It may be that you don't have to lease this building, as romantic as it sounds. You could rent a space at a retirement center or local school, at least initially, invest in the equipment to host pottery classes, build up word of mouth or an online presence and see how much demand is out there. That way, you won't be locked into a lease if the demand is not there. It will also help you envision what success means to you. Is it teaching a twice-weekly class? Or running a full-time studio?

You raise a great point when you say your retirement is not about doing nothing, or spending all of your time on the golf course or tennis court, or sitting in your garden reading - rather, it's about pursuing work that fulfills you. If pottery is a vocation for you, you have earned the right to at least look into it, given that you have worked for probably 40-plus years in jobs that helped you and your husband build a $2.9 million nest egg, even if those jobs were not your first choice.

For what it's worth, your business plan should include projected costs, including the lease, insurance, equipment, advertising, branding and marketing; projected revenue; the target market (there may be schools or senior centers nearby that would jump at the opportunity for their community to learn pottery); and, of course, the competition (find out if there are similar businesses in your area and, if so, how close they are and what they charge for classes).

Related: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Running the numbers

You won't win this argument on statements that your husband is the proverbial pot calling the kettle black, and you may not "win" the argument at all. But you will lend more credence to your pottery studio idea through data. You have $2.9 million for retirement, a mortgage-free house worth $900,000, hardly any debt, a husband who has already retired, Social Security coming down the pike, and you continue to work part-time, although that may have to end if you set up this studio.

To put your small business in context: Startup costs of $100,000 represent 3.45% of your retirement account balance. That's not nothing, but neither is it an outrageous, extravagant risk, particularly given that this is an investment to further a pastime that brings you joy and, hopefully, makes money. What is your annual income now? What will it be in five years? What are your annual expenses? How much of your retirement is in traditional accounts versus Roth?

Another missing piece of this puzzle: Do you have a "fun money" account, an emergency fund or CDs or bonds to draw from? Otherwise, you would have to take this money from your investments. That would mean you need to take more than $100,000, because you would have to pay tax on the money you withdraw from a traditional IRA or 401(k). You would lose future investment returns (which you would ideally recoup, even if only in part, from your studio).

A $100,000 startup cost represents 3.45% of your retirement-account balance.

Tell your husband that you're not giving up before you've even started, just as you would not expect him to give up on a passion project without at least stress-testing the finances. The unspoken part of this conversation, particularly after his motorboat project, is hanging over you. It does not sound like you are asking him for permission, per se - rather, you are requesting his support, and I assume you have both contributed to your retirement fund, either as a corporate worker or a homemaker.

Agree on a maximum amount you can afford to lose on a studio. You will need working capital, particularly in the early stages, when you are building your reputation. This is an opportunity to step back and ask what you want from retirement. How do you want to spend your savings? What kind of issues require unanimous agreement? (Did you agree to the motorboat purchase, for instance?) How will you navigate such issues while respecting each other's space?

A woman named Kyla Glendenning opened up a pottery studio in Fort Lauderdale and said she had revenue of $71,000 in the first six months, but spent nearly $20,000 on Facebook advertisements. That tells me, in addition to the costs of setting up a studio, signing a lease and buying equipment, that your biggest challenges will be getting the word out that you exist. Her online tutorials and videos on social media - where I found her - also require both time and money.

Don't let anyone crack your bowls before they've even hit the kiln.

By Philip van Doorn

Also in Weekend Reads: Full coverage of the Anthropic IPO, the 'death cross' for small-cap stocks and advice from The Moneyist

Take-Two Interactive owns Rockstar Games, the developer of the "Grand Theft Auto" series of videogames.

"Grand Theft Auto VI" was released by Rockstar Games on Thursday for the PlayStation 5 and Microsoft Xbox Series X and Series S consoles. The reviews for the latest entry in the game series - coming 13 years after the launch of "GTA V" - have been overwhelmingly positive.

So now you might wonder whether or not it is too late to make a long-term investment in Take-Two Interactive Software (TTWO), which owns Rockstar Games. And it might surprise you that Take-Two's stock was down 18.5% for 2026, and had lost 8.4% for the week, through Thursday. Then again, the stock had risen 39.1% in 2025 as investors anticipated the "GTA 6" release, which was delayed.

Bill Peters looked into the reasons investors have sold-off Take-Two's stock, even as the company booked $2.36 billion in pre-orders for "GTA 6."

The sales cycle for "GTA 6" is expected to stretch over several years. While it has been released on two console platforms, Rockstar hasn't said when the game will be released on PCs.

Take-Two's stock closed at $208.65 on Thursday, and its forward price/earnings ratio was 23.6, based on the consensus 12-month earnings-per-share estimate of $8.86 among analysts polled by FactSet. That forward P/E compares with a weighted valuation of 17.3 for the S&P 500 SPX.

The stock might appear to be a bit pricey. But if we look at full-year estimates, the company's earnings per share are expected to increase at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 28.9% from calendar 2026 through 2028. And that earnings growth is expected to follow this year's profit boost from the "GTA 6" release.

The projected EPS CAGR for the S&P 500 from 2026 through 2028 is 16.9%. Per the P/E valuations, investors aren't paying a high premium for Take-Two when compared with the index.

Pinnacol Assurance Wins Denver Metro Chamber's Business Impact Award for Corporate Social Responsibility

PR Newswire

DENVER, Nov. 20, 2026

Colorado's largest workers' compensation insurer recognized for investing in families, workforce development and community nonprofits

DENVER, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce named Pinnacol Assurance as the winner of their Business Impact Award in the Corporate Social Responsibility category. The awards recognize "the businesses shaping Colorado's economy and creating a stronger future."

Pinnacol, a home-grown, member-owned workers' comp carrier that has protected Colorado workers and employers for more than 110 years, was recognized for investing in the communities it serves, from scholarships for families affected by workplace tragedy to workforce development for underrepresented Coloradans.

"Pinnacol was created to protect Colorado workers and businesses, and we believe that responsibility doesn't end when a claim closes," said Pinnacol President and CEO, John O'Donnell. "This recognition belongs to our employees, who make a difference for Colorado families, students, and small businesses. We're grateful to the Denver Metro Chamber for this recognition, and we're committed to doing even more."

"Pinnacol Assurance is a fantastic organization, and it shows in everything they do," said Raymond H. Gonzales, Executive Vice President of the Denver Metro Chamber and Interim President of the Chamber Leadership Foundation. "Their approach to corporate social responsibility isn't a side project. It's woven into how they operate, from the culture they've built for their own employees to the impact they make in communities across Colorado. That kind of commitment creates a ripple effect, spreading positivity inside the company and far beyond its walls. Pinnacol is exactly the kind of leader this award was created to celebrate."

Supporting Colorado families and workers

Through the Pinnacol Foundation, Pinnacol has awarded nearly $8 million in scholarships to more than 800 Colorado students since 2001, making it the largest program of its kind in the country. The scholarships go to children whose parents were seriously injured or killed on the job, whether or not the parent was insured by Pinnacol. In 2025-26, 86 students received more than $400,000.

Building Colorado's workforce

In 2025, 76% of Pinnacol's community investments supported workforce development in underrepresented communities. Those investments helped more than 5,700 students and adult learners pursue career pathways. Participants earned more than 5,500 credentials, and more than 650 graduates entered construction jobs.

Pinnacol also awarded $265,622 to 16 Colorado nonprofits in 2025, including the Foundation for Colorado Community Colleges, Mi Casa Resource Center, CrossPurpose and the Construction Education Foundation of Colorado.

In the last decade, Pinnacol's youth apprenticeship program has employed 83 paid apprentices from eight school districts and 24 high schools. About 30% have converted to full-time Pinnacol employees. The model has been studied by state delegations, federal policymakers and educators, and in 2025 the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment honored Pinnacol with its Creating Tomorrow's Workforce Today Award.

Employees giving back

Pinnacol employees receive unlimited paid time to volunteer. In 2025, they contributed more than 2,500 hours to 104 Colorado nonprofits, including 708 hours supporting veterans and disabled veterans. Through Pinnacol in Action, employees have given more than 80,000 volunteer hours over two decades.

Employee giving is also strong. In 2025, an astounding 82.3% of employees participated in the company's giving campaign, donating $175,044. Pinnacol matched those gifts, bringing the total to $350,089 for nonprofits serving our community.

Turning recovery into service

Pinnacol's Return to Work Volunteering Program connects injured workers who can't yet return to their regular jobs with nonprofits for modified-duty work. Participants have contributed approximately 14,000 volunteer hours across Colorado, keeping workers active and connected while nonprofits gain extra help.

Learn more about how Pinnacol is a Force for Good in Colorado.

We offer top-rated injured worker care, customized safety solutions, and a comprehensive return-to-work program that helps our members reduce risk and save costs. You can see our investment in the community through our nationally recognized apprenticeship program and Pinnacol Foundation scholarship program. Pinnacol's team members, culture of caring and top-rated services have received numerous awards, affirming our commitment to the people and communities we serve. Learn more at Pinnacol.com.
